text_to_speech: So here is the structure of Rubisco. It doesn't look like a pacman, it doesn't look like a rubik's cube. It actually is quite complex. It's quite a large enzyme complex. The reason for that is because it's actually made of 16 different proteins. So we have subunits (of) which eight are grey here - so you can see the difference - and then we've got green subunits at the top and the bottom. So together, these 16 proteins actually constitute 4800 amino acids to make up this enzyme called Rubisco. Now as (I) indicated this is the most abundant enzyme in the world and for us it's also the most important. So the question is: how big is Rubisco then? Well in actual fact if you wanted to just - if you lined up 70,000 Rubisco molecules side to side here, then they would actually spread one millimeter. So proteins and enzymes are actually very very small even those which are quite large like Rubisco. Now we also talked about the catalytic sites now the thing about Rubisco is it doesn't have just one catalytic site, it actually has eight for every molecule. And the reactions carried out by Rubisco is ... So what happens at each of these eight catalytic sites is Rubisco initiates the conversion of carbon dioxide into sugars and as we know, sugars comprise carbon, hydrogen and oxygen So the carbon and the oxygen in these sugars comes from the CO₂, fixed by Rubisco and the hydrogen actually comes from water.

It actually is quite complex. It's quite a large enzyme complex. The reason for that is because it's actually made of 16 different proteins.
So we have subunits which are 8 are gray here so you can see the difference and then we've got green subunits at the top and the bottom.

Now as indicated this is the most abundant enzyme in the world and for us it's also the most important.
So the question is how big is Rubisco then? Well in actual fact if you lined up 70,000 Rubisco molecules side to side here,
then they would actually spread 1mm. So proteins and enzymes are actually very very small even those which are quite large like Rubisco.
Now we also talked about the catalytic sites. Now the thing about Rubisco is it doesn't have just one catalytic site.
It actually has 8 for every molecule. And the reactions carried out by Rubisco is...
So what happens at each of these 8 catalytic sites is Rubisco initiates the conversion of carbon dioxide into sugars.
And as we know sugars comprise carbon hydrogen oxygen. So the carbon on the oxygen in these sugars comes from the CO2 fixed by Rubisco and the hydrogen actually comes from water.

youtube_description:
Relevant to curriculum descriptors: ACSBL050 - Biochemical processes in the cell are controlled by the nature and arrangement of internal membranes, the presence of specific enzymes, and environmental factors.
ACSBL051 - Enzymes have specific functions, which can be affected by factors including temperature, pH, the presence of inhibitors, and the concentrations of reactants and products.

Created by the ARC Centre of Excellence for Translational Photosynthesis. Presented by Professor Spencer Whitney. 

Spencer’s research focuses on utilising novel biotechnological tools to scrutinize the biology of the biospheres most abundant protein, the photosynthetic Carbon dioxide-fixing enzyme Rubisco.
Spencer undertook his Bachelor of Science (Honours) and PhD at James Cook University.
From 2004 to 2009 he held an ARC Research Fellowship and from 2009 to 2013 held an ARC Future Fellowship.
